questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Affordability, vibrant city, opportunities to improve language abilities

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: My host university had quite a few workshops/meetings for international students in the beginning.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an international students coordinator we could contact. I had a zoom-meting with them, they were helpful with information about rules and courses.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: We had a nice apartment with a friendly and helpful landlord that we knew through a friend who had previously stayed there. But I know others have not been so lucky!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: To research the place/area beforehand, to start looking for off-campus housing very early (like minimum 3 months early).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We could sign up for a lot of courses and attend them during an initial period. Then at some point you had to discard the courses you did not want. However the course would start from the beginning, so if you jumped on a course just before the deadline you might be behind.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: the international students coordinator was helpful, but I sorted it out by myself mostly.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Quite. There was a very long waitlist for one particular course I wanted, but I wrote directly to the department and after applying in some roundabout way two times I got in. You have to take contact a lot of times and not just rely on the numbers on the screen. Oftentimes there is a way in.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: To look at the syllabus online if you can find it, and ask former exchange students from your degree what their experience was with a particular course. You also want to think about whether you want a course with a high workload or low, a final exam or not, and so on. All can be found in the syllabus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Before I got there I had heard that 300 level courses were easier than what they would be at my home university. I found this to be somewhat true intellectually, but the workload and memorization was correspondingly higher. So in the end, the toughest courses/the ones I spent the most time and energy on where actually my 300 courses, while my 400 course was more of a breeze.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The lectures were similar, but there were almost no workshops/regnetimer where you would work with the material in groups or anything similar; only lectures. So you had to spend a lot of time working and reading on your own if you did not have a study group. There were also a lot of quizzes that counted towards your final grade; this would force you to keep up with the material in a way that UCPH does not.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FRSL 211 Oral and Written French
MIMM 324 Fundamental Virology
PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology
PSYC 311 Human Cognition and the Brain

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
PSYC 311 Human Cognition and the Brain was very interesting and full of "aha" moments, but had a big memorization load. However I found the memorization to be easier because it was interesting, and you could relate things to your own body and the cases introduced. 
PHGY 488 Stem Cell Biology is nice because they don't require you to do neither quizzes nor midterm, but you must follow the lectures since they are rarely recorded. It is small course, so you have better opportunities to ask questions and engage.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The frosh (introductory days with acitvities) cost almost 1000kr for a ticket no matter which type of frosh you choose. I would recommend going on the MOC (McGill Outdoor Club) frosh, as it costs the same as the faculty frosh, but you get to go out into nature and do some adventurous stuff compared to the faculty frosh that is centered around drinking (and where people are two or three years young than you).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are expensive in Canada. Cheese especially, tofu less so. Going and eating out and going to cafés is maybe 10-20% cheaper than in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A big recreational center with gym, teamsports, yoga, squash, you name it. All for a fee, but not a crazy one. Several clubs (cultural clubs, charity clubs, music, obscure sports, games, quizzes). A mini-festival (open-air pub) in september.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would say to do some sports and to maybe join the McGill Outdoor Club if you like that sort of stuff and even if you don't. They do hikes, canoe-trips, camping, skiing, climbing, biking, apple-picking and foraging and it's all student-led.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Do some roadtrips to the country-side, maybe rent a cottage with some friends and visit maple-sirup makers, microbreweries, ice-cream factories, go hiking. You can cross the border and visit Vermont and New York State easily. In Montréal there are good opportunities to drink a beer with friends, go to concerts or go clubbing, however everything closes at 3:00. Visit the botanical garden, the biodome or the artificial islands.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Join clubs, talk to people in your class. Best advice if you really want to get local friends is to live at a residence or share an apartment with local students. 
I lived with Danes so I hardly got any local friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: You might need to speak some French some places. Usually you can get service in English, but some people are not very good at it and some even dislike English-speakers, however, if they can tell that you are not Canadian, they will give you a pass.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People really like going out in the summer; there's always people out and about.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- don't slack that much, if you do well on the quizzes you can have an easier time in the finals period.
- try to get out there and meet new people
- visit the surrounding areas (rest of Quebec, the US)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Keep an eye on deadlines for registrations and so on.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To live in another country, to feel independent, to meet new people and get new friends, to be away from my usual life. To learn things I might not have learned at UCPH (although some things were not interesting).

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: How tough the finals and midterm period can be

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
